    1| Configuration Handling
    2| ======================
    3| 
    4| Applications need some kind of configuration.  There are different settings
    5| you might want to change depending on the application environment like
    6| toggling the debug mode, setting the secret key, and other such
    7| environment-specific things.
    8| 
    9| The way Flask is designed usually requires the configuration to be
   10| available when the application starts up.  You can hard code the
   11| configuration in the code, which for many small applications is not
   12| actually that bad, but there are better ways.
   13| 
   14| Independent of how you load your config, there is a config object
   15| available which holds the loaded configuration values:
   16| The :attr:`~flask.Flask.config` attribute of the :class:`~flask.Flask`
   17| object.  This is the place where Flask itself puts certain configuration
   18| values and also where extensions can put their configuration values.  But
   19| this is also where you can have your own configuration.
   20| 
   21| 
   22| Configuration Basics
   23| --------------------
   24| 
   25| The :attr:`~flask.Flask.config` is actually a subclass of a dictionary and
   26| can be modified just like any dictionary::
   27| 
   28|     app = Flask(__name__)
   29|     app.config['TESTING'] = True
   30| 
   31| Certain configuration values are also forwarded to the
   32| :attr:`~flask.Flask` object so you can read and write them from there::
   33| 
   34|     app.testing = True
   35| 
   36| To update multiple keys at once you can use the :meth:`dict.update`
   37| method::
   38| 
   39|     app.config.update(
   40|         TESTING=True,
   41|         SECRET_KEY='192b9bdd22ab9ed4d12e236c78afcb9a393ec15f71bbf5dc987d54727823bcbf'
   42|     )
   43| 
   44| 
   45| Debug Mode
[lines 48-93]
   48| The :data:`DEBUG` config value is special because it may behave inconsistently if
   49| changed after the app has begun setting up. In order to set debug mode reliably, use the
   50| ``--debug`` option on the ``flask`` or ``flask run`` command. ``flask run`` will use the
   51| interactive debugger and reloader by default in debug mode.
   52| 
   53| .. code-block:: text

   58| config or code, this is strongly discouraged. It can't be read early by the
   59| ``flask run`` command, and some systems or extensions may have already configured
   60| themselves based on a previous value.

   71|     server, an interactive debugger will be shown for unhandled exceptions, and the
   72|     server will be reloaded when code changes. The :attr:`~flask.Flask.debug` attribute
   73|     maps to this config key. This is set with the ``FLASK_DEBUG`` environment variable.
   74|     It may not behave as expected if set in code.

   76|     **Do not enable debug mode when deploying in production.**

   78|     Default: ``False``

   83|     the app's error handlers. Extensions may also change their behavior to

  663| configuration that is always loaded and part of the version control, and a
  664| separate configuration that overrides the values as necessary as mentioned
  665| in the example above::
  666| 
  667|     app = Flask(__name__)
  668|     app.config.from_object('yourapplication.default_settings')
  669|     app.config.from_envvar('YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS')
  670| 
  671| Then you just have to add a separate :file:`config.py` file and export
  672| ``YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS=/path/to/config.py`` and you are done.  However
  673| there are alternative ways as well.  For example you could use imports or
  674| subclassing.
  675| 
  676| What is very popular in the Django world is to make the import explicit in
  677| the config file by adding ``from yourapplication.default_settings
  678| import *`` to the top of the file and then overriding the changes by hand.
  679| You could also inspect an environment variable like
  680| ``YOURAPPLICATION_MODE`` and set that to `production`, `development` etc
  681| and import different hard-coded files based on that.
  682| 
  683| An interesting pattern is also to use classes and inheritance for
  684| configuration::
  685| 
  686|     class Config(object):
  687|         TESTING = False
  688| 
  689|     class ProductionConfig(Config):
  690|         DATABASE_URI = 'mysql://user@localhost/foo'
  691| 
  692|     class DevelopmentConfig(Config):
  693|         DATABASE_URI = "sqlite:////tmp/foo.db"

    1| Working with the Shell
    2| ======================
    3| 
    4| .. versionadded:: 0.3
    5| 
    6| One of the reasons everybody loves Python is the interactive shell.  It
    7| basically allows you to execute Python commands in real time and
    8| immediately get results back.  Flask itself does not come with an
    9| interactive shell, because it does not require any specific setup upfront,
   10| just import your application and start playing around.
   11| 
   12| There are however some handy helpers to make playing around in the shell a
   13| more pleasant experience.  The main issue with interactive console
   14| sessions is that you're not triggering a request like a browser does which
   15| means that :data:`~flask.g`, :data:`~flask.request` and others are not
   16| available.  But the code you want to test might depend on them, so what
   17| can you do?
   18| 
   19| This is where some helper functions come in handy.  Keep in mind however
   20| that these functions are not only there for interactive shell usage, but
   21| also for unit testing and other situations that require a faked request
   22| context.
   23| 
   24| Generally it's recommended that you read :doc:`reqcontext` first.
   25| 
   26| Command Line Interface
   27| ----------------------
   28| 
   29| Starting with Flask 0.11 the recommended way to work with the shell is the
   30| ``flask shell`` command which does a lot of this automatically for you.
   31| For instance the shell is automatically initialized with a loaded
   32| application context.
   33| 
   34| For more information see :doc:`/cli`.
   35| 
   36| Creating a Request Context
   37| --------------------------
   38| 
   39| The easiest way to create a proper request context from the shell is by
   40| using the :attr:`~flask.Flask.test_request_context` method which creates
   41| us a :class:`~flask.ctx.RequestContext`:
   42| 
   43| >>> ctx = app.test_request_context()
   44| 
   45| Normally you would use the ``with`` statement to make this request object
   46| active, but in the shell it's easier to use the
   47| :meth:`~flask.ctx.RequestContext.push` and
   48| :meth:`~flask.ctx.RequestContext.pop` methods by hand:
   49| 
   50| >>> ctx.push()
   51| 
   52| From that point onwards you can work with the request object until you
   53| call `pop`:
   54| 
   55| >>> ctx.pop()
   56| 
   57| Firing Before/After Request
   58| ---------------------------
   59| 
   60| By just creating a request context, you still don't have run the code that
   61| is normally run before a request.  This might result in your database
   62| being unavailable if you are connecting to the database in a
   63| before-request callback or the current user not being stored on the
   64| :data:`~flask.g` object etc.
   65| 
   66| This however can easily be done yourself.  Just call
   67| :meth:`~flask.Flask.preprocess_request`:
   68| 
   69| >>> ctx = app.test_request_context()
   70| >>> ctx.push()
   71| >>> app.preprocess_request()
   72| 
   73| Keep in mind that the :meth:`~flask.Flask.preprocess_request` function
   74| might return a response object, in that case just ignore it.

  421| Application Context
  422| ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
  423| 
  424| Commands added using the Flask app's :attr:`~Flask.cli` or
  425| :class:`~flask.cli.FlaskGroup` :meth:`~cli.AppGroup.command` decorator
  426| will be executed with an application context pushed, so your custom
  427| commands and parameters have access to the app and its configuration. The
  428| :func:`~cli.with_appcontext` decorator can be used to get the same
  429| behavior, but is not needed in most cases.
  430| 
  431| .. code-block:: python
  432| 
  433|     import click
  434|     from flask.cli import with_appcontext
  435| 
  436|     @click.command()
  437|     @with_appcontext
  438|     def do_work():
  439|         ...
  440| 
  441|     app.cli.add_command(do_work)
  442| 
  443| 
  444| Plugins
  445| -------
  446| 
  447| Flask will automatically load commands specified in the ``flask.commands``
  448| `entry point`_. This is useful for extensions that want to add commands when
  449| they are installed. Entry points are specified in :file:`pyproject.toml`:
  450| 
  451| .. code-block:: toml
  452| 
  453|     [project.entry-points."flask.commands"]
  454|     my-command = "my_extension.commands:cli"
  455| 
  456| .. _entry point: https://packaging.python.org/tutorials/packaging-projects/#entry-points
  457| 
  458| Inside :file:`my_extension/commands.py` you can then export a Click
  459| object::
  460| 
  461|     import click
  462| 
  463|     @click.command()
  464|     def cli():
  465|         ...
  466| 
  467| Once that package is installed in the same virtualenv as your Flask project,
  468| you can run ``flask my-command`` to invoke the command.
  469| 
  470|

  472| 
  473| Custom Scripts
  474| --------------
  475| 
  476| When you are using the app factory pattern, it may be more convenient to define
  477| your own Click script. Instead of using ``--app`` and letting Flask load
  478| your application, you can create your own Click object and export it as a
  479| `console script`_ entry point.
  480| 
  481| Create an instance of :class:`~cli.FlaskGroup` and pass it the factory::
  482| 
  483|     import click

    1| Configuration Handling
    2| ======================
    3| 
    4| Applications need some kind of configuration.  There are different settings
    5| you might want to change depending on the application environment like
    6| toggling the debug mode, setting the secret key, and other such
    7| environment-specific things.
    8| 
    9| The way Flask is designed usually requires the configuration to be
   10| available when the application starts up.  You can hard code the
   11| configuration in the code, which for many small applications is not
   12| actually that bad, but there are better ways.
   13| 
   14| Independent of how you load your config, there is a config object
   15| available which holds the loaded configuration values:
   16| The :attr:`~flask.Flask.config` attribute of the :class:`~flask.Flask`
   17| object.  This is the place where Flask itself puts certain configuration
   18| values and also where extensions can put their configuration values.  But
   19| this is also where you can have your own configuration.
   20| 
   21| 
   22| Configuration Basics
   23| --------------------
   24| 
   25| The :attr:`~flask.Flask.config` is actually a subclass of a dictionary and
   26| can be modified just like any dictionary::
   27| 
   28|     app = Flask(__name__)
   29|     app.config['TESTING'] = True
   30| 
   31| Certain configuration values are also forwarded to the
   32| :attr:`~flask.Flask` object so you can read and write them from there::
   33| 
   34|     app.testing = True
   35| 
   36| To update multiple keys at once you can use the :meth:`dict.update`
   37| method::
   38| 
   39|     app.config.update(
   40|         TESTING=True,
   41|         SECRET_KEY='192b9bdd22ab9ed4d12e236c78afcb9a393ec15f71bbf5dc987d54727823bcbf'
   42|     )
   43| 
   44|

[lines 48-93]
   48| The :data:`DEBUG` config value is special because it may behave inconsistently if
   49| changed after the app has begun setting up. In order to set debug mode reliably, use the
   50| ``--debug`` option on the ``flask`` or ``flask run`` command. ``flask run`` will use the
   51| interactive debugger and reloader by default in debug mode.
   52| 
   53| .. code-block:: text
   54| 
   55|     $ flask --app hello run --debug
   56| 
   57| Using the option is recommended. While it is possible to set :data:`DEBUG` in your
   58| config or code, this is strongly discouraged. It can't be read early by the
   59| ``flask run`` command, and some systems or extensions may have already configured
   60| themselves based on a previous value.
   61| 
   62| 
   63| Builtin Configuration Values
   64| ----------------------------
   65| 
   66| The following configuration values are used internally by Flask:
   67| 
   68| .. py:data:: DEBUG
   69| 
   70|     Whether debug mode is enabled. When using ``flask run`` to start the development
   71|     server, an interactive debugger will be shown for unhandled exceptions, and the
   72|     server will be reloaded when code changes. The :attr:`~flask.Flask.debug` attribute
   73|     maps to this config key. This is set with the ``FLASK_DEBUG`` environment variable.
   74|     It may not behave as expected if set in code.
   75| 
   76|     **Do not enable debug mode when deploying in production.**
   77| 
   78|     Default: ``False``
   79| 
   80| .. py:data:: TESTING
   81| 
   82|     Enable testing mode. Exceptions are propagated rather than handled by the
   83|     the app's error handlers. Extensions may also change their behavior to
   84|     facilitate easier testing. You should enable this in your own tests.
   85| 
   86|     Default: ``False``
   87| 
   88| .. py:data:: PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS
   89| 
   90|     Exceptions are re-raised rather than being handled by the app's error
   91|     handlers. If not set, this is implicitly true if ``TESTING`` or ``DEBUG``
   92|     is enabled.

  522| Configuring from Data Files
  523| ---------------------------
  524| 
  525| It is also possible to load configuration from a file in a format of

  527| from a TOML file:

  655| .. _config-dev-prod:
  656| 
  657| Development / Production
  658| ------------------------
  659| 
  660| Most applications need more than one configuration.  There should be at
  661| least separate configurations for the production server and the one used
  662| during development.  The easiest way to handle this is to use a default
  663| configuration that is always loaded and part of the version control, and a
  664| separate configuration that overrides the values as necessary as mentioned
  665| in the example above::
  666| 
  667|     app = Flask(__name__)
  668|     app.config.from_object('yourapplication.default_settings')
  669|     app.config.from_envvar('YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS')
  670| 
  671| Then you just have to add a separate :file:`config.py` file and export
  672| ``YOURAPPLICATION_SETTINGS=/path/to/config.py`` and you are done.  However
  673| there are alternative ways as well.  For example you could use imports or
  674| subclassing.
  675| 
  676| What is very popular in the Django world is to make the import explicit in
  677| the config file by adding ``from yourapplication.default_settings
  678| import *`` to the top of the file and then overriding the changes by hand.
  679| You could also inspect an environment variable like
  680| ``YOURAPPLICATION_MODE`` and set that to `production`, `development` etc
  681| and import different hard-coded files based on that.
  682| 
  683| An interesting pattern is also to use classes and inheritance for
  684| configuration::
  685| 
  686|     class Config(object):
  687|         TESTING = False
  688| 
  689|     class ProductionConfig(Config):
  690|         DATABASE_URI = 'mysql://user@localhost/foo'
  691| 
  692|     class DevelopmentConfig(Config):
  693|         DATABASE_URI = "sqlite:////tmp/foo.db"

  521| PyCharm Integration
  522| -------------------
  523| 
  524| PyCharm Professional provides a special Flask run configuration to run the development
  525| server. For the Community Edition, and for other commands besides ``run``, you need to
  526| create a custom run configuration. These instructions should be similar for any other
  527| IDE you use.
  528| 
  529| In PyCharm, with your project open, click on *Run* from the menu bar and go to *Edit
  530| Configurations*. You'll see a screen similar to this:
  531| 
  532| .. image:: _static/pycharm-run-config.png
  533|     :align: center
  534|     :class: screenshot
  535|     :alt: Screenshot of PyCharm run configuration.
  536| 
  537| Once you create a configuration for the ``flask run``, you can copy and change it to
  538| call any other command.
  539| 
  540| Click the *+ (Add New Configuration)* button and select *Python*. Give the configuration
  541| a name such as "flask run".
  542| 
  543| Click the *Script path* dropdown and change it to *Module name*, then input ``flask``.
  544| 
  545| The *Parameters* field is set to the CLI command to execute along with any arguments.
  546| This example uses ``--app hello run --debug``, which will run the development server in
  547| debug mode. ``--app hello`` should be the import or file with your Flask app.
  548| 
  549| If you installed your project as a package in your virtualenv, you may uncheck the
  550| *PYTHONPATH* options. This will more accurately match how you deploy later.
  551| 
  552| Click *OK* to save and close the configuration. Select the configuration in the main
  553| PyCharm window and click the play button next to it to run the server.
  554| 
  555| Now that you have a configuration for ``flask run``, you can copy that configuration and
  556| change the *Parameters* argument to run a different CLI command.

Custom Scripts
--------------

When you are using the app factory pattern, it may be more convenient to define
your own Click script. Instead of using ``--app`` and letting Flask load
your application, you can create your own Click object and export it as a
`console script`_ entry point.

Create an instance of :class:`~cli.FlaskGroup` and pass it the factory::

    import click
    from flask import Flask
    from flask.cli import FlaskGroup

    def create_app():
        app = Flask('wiki')
        # other setup
        return app

    @click.group(cls=FlaskGroup, create_app=create_app)
    def cli():
        """Management script for the Wiki application."""

Define the entry point in :file:`pyproject.toml`:

.. code-block:: toml

    [project.scripts]
    wiki = "wiki:cli"

Install the application in the virtualenv in editable mode and the custom
script is available. Note that you don't need to set ``--app``. ::

    $ pip install -e .
    $ wiki run

.. admonition:: Errors in Custom Scripts

    When using a custom script, if you introduce an error in your
    module-level code, the reloader will fail because it can no longer
    load the entry point.

    The ``flask`` command, being separate from your code, does not have
    this issue and is recommended in most cases.

.. _console script: https://packaging.python.org/tutorials/packaging-projects/#console-scripts


Configuring the Application
---------------------------

You can print the loaded configuration for the application using the ``config``
command. This will print the configuration as JSON, masking any values that
contain "SECRET", "PASSWORD", "TOKEN", or "KEY". ::

    $ flask config
    {
        "DEBUG": false,
        "SECRET_KEY": "***",
        ...
    }
